Perhaps I should start this with the ubiquitous disclaimer that I love my kids. It's terrific, and I think I can say without hesitation that I love my kids more than I've ever loved anything before. I love my kids more than I love myself. I love my kids more than I love my wife. I love my kids more than I loved my mom when I was 8, and I skinned my knee. All I want for my kid is for them to have the happiest lives that's possible in this world.

A lot of this falls on me... my basic parental responsibilities... to make sure they have adequate access to nutritious foods, health care, stimulating entertainment, social outlets, education, clothes, medicine, toys, car seats, maybe some form of college fund, etc... Most importantly, they need our love, out attention, and, if possible, to have someone in their lives that thinks they're just the bees-knees, the best thing since sliced bread, an ally and a mentor in the face of the world.

But here's the wild card. Here's where all of that simple stuff fades away into a realm that's much more complicated and tears at the soul of every parent who gives a damn: how much is our job is to change who they are?

It would be easy... so easy... to let them write the script. Give them any food they want, let them play or do anything they wand. Let them watch what they want, sleep when they want, have anything they asked for whenever it were possible. However, almost any parent would say that a parent who did that would be awful. You'd raise a spoiled brat, right? That's what we expect anyway.

So there in lies the beginning of the eternal parenting conflict. How much of what we're trying to do is to defy and change our kids? We want them to eat healthy so they grow strong and fit. We want them to engage with enriching media so they get smart and curious. We regulate their behavior so that they learn to be courteous and kind. We make them take naps so they don't get all moody in the afternoon. We do all these things for the same reason: we want them to be happy. When we defy their wishes, it's for their long-term benefit. They'll thank us for this later... we hope.

But, where do you draw the line?

It's probably a fuzzy line. We've already established that being totally laissez-faire is probably not the right way, and I won't even bother elaborating on how one could err on the other side of that coin. Suffice to say, ruling over your children with an iron fist can be taken too far. So, where's the middle ground. How much do you sacrifice making your kid momentarily happy for the sake of trying to train them to act a certain way, and how much are you trying to change?

Are you just trying to get your kids to "behave" and follow the rules? Are you identifying certain personality traits and trying to actively "mold" their personality? Are you training them skills and trying to teach them how to do lots of things? Are you trying to give them a good taste in movies or music? How much is the right amount to deliberately affect their behavior?

This is an open question, and I don't have the answer. I'm asking this question because I'm trying to find a balance. I guess the reason it's perplexing me is because I'm not sure where that line is. I have a kid who's got some issues... don't we all. He has a tendency to get really upset at relatively minor things. He's not quite four, but I see lots of kids his age, and he's a little bit on the sensitive side.

When he gets sad, is it just my job to console him and to be nice to him... or is it my job to leverage these occasions to make him stronger? If I think of the most effective way I could possible make him happy, I can think of a bunch of stuff. But when I think of the most effective things I could do and say to compel him to learn to suppress those emotions and to learn to be more in control of his feelings, it's a totally different set of things.

And, is it even possible to change who someone is. Can you train a child to be more stoic and reserved, or are kids just who they're going to be no matter what you do?

I'm still not sure, but I'd love to hear what anyone thought about the subject.

I think the thing to keep in mind is that all of us are shaped by the world we live in, and this school of ours is one of hard knocks. You want your kids to be happy, and oftentimes, being 'happy' has a lot less to do with getting exactly what you want, and a lot more to do with how much you get jerked around by the short leash life keeps you on. When you imagine your 'nightmare scenario' for your adult children, regardless of the exact particulars, I think the single thing that's a common thread for every parent is regret. You don't want to see your kid in their 30's or 40's, suffering the consequences of their poor decisions, and regretful of all the paths they've gone down to get there.

In that sense, then, 'molding' your child is something you have to do--but you have to do it as a 'prosthetic' for life, communicating the lessons that your child has the opportunity to learn, but that they wouldn't due to their naivety and youthful lack of attention span.

As an example, your child will at some point have spending power. That spending power will be much more limited than your spending power as their parent, because of course it will. So, rather than having an item-by-item approval process with your child, you should encourage them to make decisions between things that they want. Instead of holding the transactional power, "dad wouldn't buy me that, dad would buy me this", make sure that they don't have enough money to buy everything they want, but that they have enough to buy some: "dad gave me this much allowance, and I want these skates more than I want those jeans".

Is it even possible to change who someone is?

I would vote no, it is not. It is possible to change who you yourself are, though. You may not be able to imbue your child with stoicism--but you can, and should, work with them to make sure they adopt or reject stoicism based on the reality, based on the facts about what consequences it will have for them.

You may not be able to dictate what your child wants. But, you can absolutely make sure that their ability to execute, that their ability to follow through and to select their future from the list of possible things for them--not just to be moths near a votive stand.
